checkpoints: Session = remembering: an in-memory or central session store is wiped on server restart, losing all logged-in state.
Behind a load balancer with multiple instances, a session model needs sticky sessions or a shared-store lookup on every request — meaning every request pays a store round-trip cost.
JWT = verifying: the server signs a self-contained token (header.payload.signature) carrying claims like sub (user id) and exp (expiry).
Verification happens locally by recomputing the HMAC with the shared secret and checking exp — a cheap operation with zero lookups.
Consequence: any instance holding the secret can authenticate any token, so the system scales horizontally with no shared session store.
The honest price of statelessness: nothing is stored, so nothing can be revoked before exp — a leaked token lives out its full TTL.
That is a designed trade-off, and exactly what the refresh-token mechanism resolves.
Authentication answers 'who are you': check the token's signature and expiry, then attach identity plus its role to the request.
Authorization answers 'what may you do': compare that attached role against the roles the route declares allowed.
The order is fixed — authenticate first, authorize second — because authorization reads exactly what authentication just produced; you cannot compare a role you don't yet know.
No token at all -> the authentication layer stops it right there, returning 401, since the system doesn't yet know who you are.
A valid token with role user -> clears authentication but loses the role comparison, returning 403, since identity is known but permission is lacking.
An admin token -> clears both layers, returning 200.
Merging the two layers collapses the logic into 'valid token = access to anything,' letting any logged-in user reach every route, including admin ones.
Keeping the two codes distinct drives the right client behavior: hit a 401, re-authenticate; hit a 403, stop — re-logging in fixes nothing.

Linking a new sign-in identity to an existing account by email alone is only safe when the provider returning that email is the same provider that already verified it for that account - a different provider reporting the same email is attacker-controllable and must not be trusted as proof of ownership.

The Google callback's email fallback is safe specifically because Google verifies the email before OAuth completes; reusing that same lookup-by-email-and-link logic in a shared handler for a second provider like GitHub carries that assumption somewhere it no longer holds.

The exploit requires no access to the victim's real accounts: an attacker registers a GitHub identity using the victim's email address, drives the OAuth callback, gets matched to the victim's row purely by email, has their githubId silently written onto that row, and is issued a session as the victim.

A safe identity model uses a stable provider-scoped id (like githubId) as the primary re-login match, and treats email only as a deliberate, opt-in link key - a cross-provider or unverified email match should require the user to explicitly confirm the link while already authenticated, not silently attach a new provider id and issue a session.

Gating a mock or offline login path purely on a runtime config flag (like MOCK_GITHUB) is not an environment boundary, because a single misconfigured or leaked environment variable can flip it on in production; a test-only auth bypass needs to be structurally unreachable outside dev/test (build-time exclusion or equivalent), not merely defaulted to false.

Reviewing this kind of change at the design level means naming the actual security contract being broken - the identity-convergence key hierarchy of provider-id-first matching with email as a guarded link key - rather than commenting on individual lines of the diff.

Before approving the PR, the fix should reorder matching to check githubId first (mirroring the Google flow), require an authenticated confirmation step for any email collision without a githubId match, and condition that confirmation on the provider's own email-verified claim being true.

The required test coverage before merge includes: an unverified or different-provider email must not auto-link and should instead return a pending-confirmation response rather than a session token; a repeat callback for the same githubId must converge on the single existing row without creating a duplicate; and a production-configuration test must assert the mock login branch is unreachable.

A hot path with three stacked costs should be profiled and ranked by actual impact rather than fixed in file order — the exponential bcrypt cost dominates the ~1s p95, while the sequential token signing and the duplicate user fetch are smaller, still-worthwhile wins on top.

Bcrypt's cost factor is exponential, so raising it from a baseline of 10 to 15 is not a modest bump but roughly 2^5 = 32x the hashing work, which alone plausibly explains most of the observed latency regression.

The bcrypt work factor exists to make brute-forcing a low-entropy secret like a human-chosen password expensive; a refresh token is a long, cryptographically random string with entropy far beyond what any cost factor needs to defend, so hashing it at cost 15 buys no real security margin and should be dropped back to the lesson's baseline of 10.

Signing the access token and the refresh token are independent operations with no data dependency between them, so awaiting them one after another wastes wall-clock time that `Promise.all` can reclaim by running both signs concurrently.

The refresh guard's strategy (`RtStrategy.validate`) already loads the full user row while authenticating the caller, so having the service re-fetch that same row by id is a redundant database round trip that can be eliminated by forwarding the guard-validated user object into the service instead of just its id.

None of the three latency fixes should touch the security-relevant invariants of refresh-token rotation: the raw refresh token is still never persisted (only its bcrypt hash reaches the database), a successful rotation still overwrites the stored hash, and a replayed, already-rotated token still fails the bcrypt compare and is rejected.

Optimizations to a security-sensitive hot path should be verified with a before/after p95 measurement on the refresh endpoint to confirm the latency win, combined with the existing behavioral suite (fresh token pair on rotation, 401 on replayed old tokens, hash cleared on logout) and a query-log check showing one fewer `findOne` call per refresh to confirm the duplicate fetch was actually removed.

The steady-state workload is dominated by returning, already-linked users, so the login path should be optimized for one read and zero writes in that common case rather than for the first-login or linking edge cases.

Two sequential `findOne` calls — first by provider id, then by email — reserve a full extra round trip on every login even though the email fallback almost never fires for users who are already linked.
TypeORM's array-form `where` clause expresses OR, so both the provider-id key and the email key can be checked in a single query instead of two sequential queries.

When one OR query can match on either key, the old sequential priority — provider-id match beats email match — has to be re-applied in memory over the returned candidates to preserve the original linking precedence.

Reassigning `user.googleId = payload.googleId` and calling `save()` on every returning login triggers a full UPDATE (row lock, WAL entry, index touch) even though the value did not change, which is exactly the one-UPDATE-per-login pattern a monitoring graph would show under a login spike.

Persisting should be conditional: save only when the provider id is being linked for the first time (previously unset) or when a tracked profile field genuinely changed, turning the returning-user path into a pure read with zero writes.

Behavior parity has to hold across all three flows after the optimization: a brand-new identity still INSERTs and returns `isNewUser: true`, an existing email-only account still converges onto the same row once provider id is linked, and a returning user still resolves to that same row with `isNewUser: false`.

The optimization can be confirmed by the query log showing one query per callback instead of up to two, and by a returning-user load test showing the users-table write rate flatten toward zero while read latency drops back to the single-round-trip baseline.
Contract splits into three clean parts: one source of truth (role enum), one declaration mechanism, and one enforcement point.
Role enum (admin/editor/user/viewer) is the single constant set the whole system references, signed alongside identity into the token at sign-in so no route ever has to guess permission.

Every route declares its own permission through a purely declarative mechanism (decorator+reflector, attribute, annotation, or middleware) that only ATTACHES metadata (allowed-roles list or public flag) and checks nothing itself.

Exactly ONE centralized chain enforces permission through two ordered layers: authentication first (verify token, attach identity, fail 401 if not yet known) then authorization second (compare declared role metadata against attached identity, fail 403 if lacking permission).
This order is structurally mandatory, not a convention — authorization needs identity as its input, so running it before authentication would always yield 403 since there's nothing to compare yet.
Semantics: a multi-role list is OR (matching any one suffices); a route with no role metadata lets any authenticated user in, since only the authentication layer still gates it.

The public flag is a separate, explicit per-route opt-out that the authentication layer itself honors — never the default, and deserves its own checkpoint since it's the one case that bypasses login entirely.

Extension proof: adding a new "reports" area only needs role declarations on its new routes (plus one enum value if a genuinely new role) — the central enforcement chain is never touched because it reads metadata per route instead of hard-coding logic per route.
Core convergence rule: one human converges to exactly one user row, guaranteed by a key hierarchy that holds across multiple providers.

Architecture: each entry point (local password, Google callback, future provider callback) runs through its own normalizer that maps the provider's raw profile into one common payload shape, then hands off to a single identity-service that owns the entire convergence logic — never scattered across handlers.
password is NULLABLE for OAuth-originated accounts because the real credential lives at the provider, not the app's DB — a deliberate contract, not a validation gap.
Key hierarchy: the calling provider's own stable unique id (e.g. googleId) is by itself sufficient to re-match on re-login; email is used only as a LINK key, never to re-match.
Decision matrix, safe branch: silent linking is permitted ONLY when the identity arrives from the exact same provider that already verified that email.

Decision matrix, unsafe branch: a DIFFERENT provider or an unverified email must instead require the user to confirm the link while authenticated — and names the specific attack this blocks (an attacker who knows the victim's email registers on a different provider and auto-merges by email to take over the account).

isNewUser is derived from which identity-resolution branch fired (matched by provider id / linked by email / newly inserted), returned to the client for onboarding, and deliberately excluded from the JWT since it is a one-time login outcome, not a durable identity property.
JWT-issuance boundary: no provider's own callback may ever mint the app's JWT itself — only once the identity-service has fully converged on exactly one row does the app issue its own internal JWT.

The tampered sub token dies at verification: changing the payload means the server-recomputed HMAC (over header+payload with the server's secret) no longer matches the attached signature → 401, exactly what the lesson's tamper flow demonstrates.

This protection is only ONE-directional: base64url is an ENCODING, not an ENCRYPTION, so the attacker could still READ the payload freely (every sub, exp, ... decoded in plain sight) — they only failed to ALTER it undetected.
The teammate's proposal is wrong on its face: any client, proxy, or anyone holding the token can read every claim inside, no secret required.
Rule: the payload should only carry minimal, non-sensitive claims (sub, exp) — the signature gives integrity, but confidentiality is something a JWT never provides.
Caveat: this entire integrity guarantee only holds if the signing secret is strong and kept secret — leak it or make it weak, and forged tokens verify perfectly fine.
Check order: RtGuard verifies signature and expiry first — both pass because the token is cryptographically genuine.

AuthService then compares the raw token against the stored bcrypt hash; rotation already overwrote that hash at the previous refresh, so bcrypt.compare fails → server returns 401 "revoked or rotated", no tokens issued.
This is the single-use property rotation buys: the DB's one hash column always describes only the LATEST refresh.
Interpretation: a replayed rotated token means either client desync or theft — this is reuse detection, the main reason to rotate at all.

Escalation path: the single-column model can only refuse the one token (401); modeling tokens as a family with lineage turns the same replay into a theft PROOF, revoking the whole family and returning 403, forcing re-login everywhere — same behaviour observed, different blast radius of the response.

The "one 30-day access token" proposal collides with a core contradiction: stateless verification (no DB lookup) is exactly what makes access checks fast and horizontally scalable, and exactly what makes revocation impossible — the server has nowhere to mark a token dead.
So a 30-day access token means a 30-day unrevocable window the moment it leaks.
The split design separates the RIGHT TO ACCESS from the RIGHT TO RENEW: access lives short (~15 minutes), self-bounding the blast radius while staying fully stateless.

Refresh lives long (~7 days) to preserve UX, but is anchored to one bit of server state — the bcrypt hash stored on the user row; logout only nulls that hash and rotation overwrites it on every use, making the renewal right revocable with a single column, no global blacklist required.
Two separate signing secrets keep the two token types mutually exclusive right at the guard layer — a refresh cannot impersonate an access token.

Residual risk honestly acknowledged: even under this design a leaked access token still rides out its full ~15 minutes — the accepted price; going further with an access denylist would buy state back but trade away the original stateless advantage.
